title: Data, Charts, and Evidence
subtitle: Making the numbers do your work
outcome: Turn any dataset into a small number of claims, design charts that carry those claims honestly, and deliver the numbers out loud in a way that survives scrutiny.
abstract: Most data in executive presentations fails silently: it is presented accurately and changes nothing, because the chart was chosen from the shape of the data rather than the question, the title names the subject instead of the finding, and the audience is left to do the analysis the speaker was paid to do. This module treats evidence as a design problem with a small number of transferable moves. It covers the perceptual science that decides what an audience actually sees, from Colin Ware's preattentive attributes to Cleveland and McGill's ranking of visual channels and Tufte's data-ink ratio, and it puts the practical instruments in the room: the one-message chart, the message title, the 'so what?' annotation, the Question-to-Chart Map, the Exec Number Set, and the Data Honesty Audit. It also covers the credibility economics of getting caught, and the two verbal skills that decide whether a number lands: giving it a human frame, and volunteering the weakness in your own data before the room finds it.
objectives: Diagnose chart wallpaper and convert a subject-title chart into one that carries a single claim.
Apply preattentive attribute theory and the perceptual hierarchy to choose what the eye should catch first.
Reduce a chart to its data using Tufte's data-ink discipline and deploy sparklines where a full chart will not fit.
Select a chart form by mapping the audience's question to comparison, composition, distribution, relationship, trend, or target.
Write a finding-title and a 'so what?' annotation, and audit a chart for truncation, denominator, scale, and dual-axis distortion.

Assemble a three-to-five number Exec Number Set with one job per number, speak a number out loud with a denominator, a comparison, and a human frame, and volunteer the weakness in your own data before the room finds it.

keyTerms.definition: A chart that would be equally true with the data removed; decoration that signals rigour without carrying a claim.
Tufte's ratio of ink carrying information to total ink on a chart; the higher the ratio, the less non-data decoration the chart contains.
Tufte's term for non-data elements such as heavy grids, shadows, 3D effects, and redundant legends that consume attention and often distort values.
A word-sized, axis-free chart of a single series that shows a trend in minimal space, usually inside a table cell.
A visual feature such as colour hue, orientation, or spatial position that the eye detects in parallel and without focused attention.
Cleveland and McGill's ranking of visual channels by human accuracy, with position on a common scale most accurate and area, volume, and hue least.
The mapping from a question's shape (comparison, part-to-whole, distribution, relationship, change, target) to the chart forms that answer it.
A chart carrying exactly one claim, with a title stating the finding and an annotation stating the implication.
A chart title that states the finding rather than naming the subject, so the slide is comprehensible without the speaker.
A short line of text stating the implication, action, or caveat of a chart, in the speaker's own words.
A chart axis that does not start at zero, exaggerating differences; legitimate for lines, illegitimate for bars, and costly when undisclosed.
A chart with two independently scaled y-axes, which can be tuned to manufacture the appearance of a relationship.
The three to five numbers a board needs, each assigned exactly one job: scale, health, engine, or bet.
The countable, human referent attached to a figure, such as seven of the top hundred accounts, that gives a number a size the room can hold.

concepts.title: The Wallpaper Test: Why Most Charts in Decks Do Nothing
concepts.summary: A chart that would be equally true with the data removed is wallpaper: decoration that signals rigour without carrying a claim. Charts earn their place only when the audience could not have made the statement without them.
concepts.detail:
A chart that would be equally true with the data removed is wallpaper. Wallpaper slides are not neutral. They consume the room's attention, they signal that the speaker has data, and they raise the cost of every real number that follows. This is the most common failure in executive decks, and it is a failure of authorship rather than of design.

Three symptoms. First, the chart shows a dataset rather than a point: a line chart of monthly revenue for two years with no claim attached, so the audience is left to do the analysis you were paid to do. Second, the title names the subject instead of the finding: "Q3 Revenue" where "Q3 revenue grew 18 percent, driven entirely by two enterprise renewals" would be a message title. Third, the chart contains only information you were going to narrate anyway. If the room already knows ARR is up because you said it in the previous sentence, the chart adds nothing except time.

The test is simple and brutal. Remove the data and read the slide. If the remaining text is still a complete, accurate, and interesting statement, the chart is wallpaper. If removing the data makes the slide meaningless, the chart is doing work.

Charts fail structurally, not stylistically. The speaker is rewarded for completeness rather than clarity, so decks accumulate evidence, and the audience is forced to synthesize. Adults in rooms are pattern-matching, not analysing: they will take the first salient thing on the slide and treat it as the point whether or not it is. Your job is to have done the synthesis before the slide appears, because nobody in the room will do it for you.

The fix is not better graphics software. It is a decision made before you open a charting tool: what is the one thing this chart must make obvious? If you cannot write that sentence, you do not have a chart yet, and the honest move is to write the sentence first, then let the data tell you which chart form can carry it.

A corollary for the nervous executive: fewer charts is not less evidence. Ten charts that each make one clear point beat four charts that each make three, because the room can hold the first arrangement and cannot hold the second.

The test applies to tables too. A forty-row table is wallpaper with extra steps. A table is legitimate when the audience needs to look up specific values or check your work, and it is wallpaper when it is there to look rigorous.
principles: Before opening a charting tool, write the one sentence the chart must make obvious. If you cannot, you do not have a chart yet.
Run the wallpaper test on every slide: delete the data and read what remains. If it is still true and interesting, the chart is decoration.
Put the finding in the title, not just the subject, so the slide survives being read without you.
Cut charts that only repeat what you will say out loud; they cost the room time and buy nothing.
Aim for one claim per chart. A chart that supports three claims supports none of them in the room.

pitfalls.failure: Shipping a dense appendix chart because the room expects data, on the assumption that more evidence reads as more rigour.
pitfalls.fix: Move it to the appendix and say so: 'Detail on request.' Reserve the main deck for the two charts that change the decision.

pitfalls.failure: Labelling a chart with the subject ('Revenue by region') and expecting the room to derive the conclusion in silence.
pitfalls.fix: Retitle it as a finding: 'Revenue is concentrated: three regions are 70 percent of the total.' Then the audience knows what it is looking at.

pitfalls.failure: Piling slides until the deck exceeds its slot, and using chart density to fill the gap.
pitfalls.fix: Time-box the deck first. Every slide that is cut should be the one that repeats something else.

concepts.title: What the Eye Grabs First: Preattentive Attributes and the Perceptual Hierarchy
concepts.summary: The eye does not read charts, it pops out one feature at a time. Colin Ware's preattentive attributes tell you what gets seen without effort; Cleveland and McGill tell you which visual channel survives the longest. Encode the message in the channel the eye picks up first.
concepts.detail:
Colin Ware's framework in Information Visualization starts from a simple observation: human vision processes some features of an image in parallel and without focused attention, and others only one at a time with effort. Ware calls the effortless, parallel ones preattentive attributes. The canonical set includes colour hue, form, orientation, size, spatial position, and, importantly, enclosure, curvature, and the number of elements in a common region. A single red bar among grey bars is detected preattentively, in well under a second. A small difference in the length of two grey bars may not be noticed at all until someone goes looking.

The practical consequence: the attribute you vary is the attribute the audience sees first. If the message is "Europe is the problem", make Europe a different colour, not a different length. If the message is "we are falling behind plan", make the gap a distinct hue rather than a slightly taller bar. Decoration applied to a non-message attribute is a waste of the most powerful channel you have.

William Cleveland and Robert McGill's 1984 paper, "Graphical Perception: Theory and Experimentation Applied to the Development of Graphical Methods", adds the ranking most practitioners still use. Position along a common scale is the most accurate; position on a non-aligned scale, length, angle, area, and volume follow; colour hue and texture are the least accurate. So for a precise comparison of values, use position on a shared axis or a bar chart. Do not ask anyone to compare the areas of two pie slices or the volumes of two 3D bars, because the human perceptual system genuinely cannot do that well, however confident the person asking.

Two honest caveats. First, the perceptual accuracy rankings describe typical performance and depend on task and expertise; a trained analyst extracts more from a heatmap than a novice does. Second, the famous claim that position is the most accurate comes from controlled experiments with simple tasks, not from boardrooms. Use the ranking to rank your options, not to end a discussion.

The practical test for a chart you have already built: shrink it to thumbnail size, or squint at it. Whatever survives is what your audience will actually perceive. If what survives is not your message, the encoding is wrong, and no amount of annotation will repair it.
principles: Vary the attribute that carries your message; leave every other attribute uniform.
Use colour, position, and enclosure for preattentive pop; use length, angle, area, and volume only for lower-stakes comparisons.
Put the highest-stakes comparison on a shared positional scale, because that is where human accuracy is highest.
Thumbnail-test every chart: what survives at small size is what the room will actually see.
Use hue to mark the exception and greyscale for the context, so attention lands where you want it.

pitfalls.failure: Colour-coding categories because it looks designed, which splits attention across six hues and leaves the actual point unmarked.
pitfalls.fix: Mark only the series that carries the message in a distinct colour; render the rest in neutral greys.

pitfalls.failure: Encoding a precise comparison in area or angle, such as a pie chart for six segments, because the format looked professional.
pitfalls.fix: Convert to a sorted bar chart or dot plot, where the comparison runs on position against a common scale.

pitfalls.failure: Assuming a carefully designed chart communicates to everyone equally well.
pitfalls.fix: Test with a colleague who does not own the data; if they cannot name the point in five seconds, the encoding is failing.

concepts.title: Data-Ink, Chartjunk, and Sparklines: Tufte's Minimum Effective Chart
concepts.summary: Tufte's data-ink ratio asks what fraction of a chart's ink carries information, and the answer is usually less than a third. The working discipline is subtraction, and the most under-used instrument in executive communication is the sparkline.
concepts.detail:
Edward Tufte's The Visual Display of Quantitative Information is the standard for treating charts as an information-design problem rather than a software problem. Three ideas dominate it, and the second and third are the ones executives actually need on Monday morning.

**Data-ink ratio.** Tufte defines it as the ratio of the ink used to present information to the total ink used to present non-information. His maxim: above all else, show the data. A chart with a heavy grid, a drop shadow, a bevelled frame, a 3D effect, an eight-colour palette for four series, and a rotated axis title may carry a data-ink ratio below 0.3, which means most of the ink on the slide is doing nothing at all. Every element must earn its place: if the gridlines do not let a reader estimate a value, they are decoration; if a second y-axis does not support a claim, it is noise.

**Chartjunk.** Tufte's term for exactly that: the non-data elements, heavy gridlines, unnecessary shading, 3D perspective, decorative borders, redundant legends, that consume attention and often actively distort the data. His 3D examples are the canonical illustration, because perspective foreshortens the nearer segment so that the visual reading contradicts the printed number.

**Sparklines.** Tufte's later and more operational contribution: a tiny, word-sized, high-resolution chart of a single series, with no axes, no labels, and no legend, carrying a trend in a fraction of the space of a conventional chart. A sparkline inside a table cell lets a reader see a hundred trends at once, one per row, where a hundred small multiples would be unreadable. It is the most under-used instrument in executive communication precisely because it fits where a full chart cannot.

The discipline Tufte demands is subtraction, and subtraction is counter-cultural in senior rooms, where more slides and denser slides read as more work. The test is: what can you delete without losing the claim? Delete in this order, gridlines first, then legends, then axis labels where the scale is obvious, then borders and shadows, then any second series that does not support the message, and stop at the point where the claim stops being obvious.

One caveat worth stating plainly: Tufte's aesthetics have been contested, and the data-ink ratio is a heuristic rather than a law. Small multiples and deliberate colour use can be entirely appropriate. The defensible version of his claim is narrower and still useful: ink is a scarce resource in a room where attention is scarcer, and any element that carries neither information nor emphasis is stealing capacity from the elements that do.
principles: Audit every chart for data-ink: if an element carries no information and no emphasis, delete it.
Subtract in a fixed order, gridlines, legends, labels, borders, then non-essential series, and stop when the claim survives.
Never use 3D on a chart whose value anyone may quote; perspective makes the picture disagree with the number.
Use sparklines when you need to show a trend for many items at once in a small space.
Show the data before you style it: build the chart with a neutral palette, then add emphasis only where it serves the claim.

pitfalls.failure: Treating 'clean' as 'minimal', stripping the chart down until the audience can no longer read an approximate value off it.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the one element that allows estimation, a light reference line or a labelled axis, and delete everything else.

pitfalls.failure: Using a sparkline where the audience needs to check a specific value, because the trend was easier to produce.
pitfalls.fix: Use the sparkline for the trend and put the exact figure in the row, in text, beside it.

pitfalls.failure: Keeping a legend and direct-labelling the same series, so the reader has to reconcile two encodings of the same thing.
pitfalls.fix: Label the series directly at the end of each line and delete the legend.

concepts.title: Choosing the Form to the Question: The Question-to-Chart Map
concepts.summary: Charts fail when the form is chosen from the data type, 'we have time series, so a line chart'. Start from the question the audience needs answered, then pick the form that can answer it: comparison, part-to-whole, distribution, relationship, change over time, or rank against a target.
concepts.detail:
Most bad charts are not badly drawn. They are badly chosen, and the choice is usually made from the shape of the data rather than the shape of the question. "We have monthly revenue, so a line chart" is a data-type decision. "The board needs to know whether growth is accelerating or just steady" is a question, and the question dictates the form.

There are only a handful of question shapes, and each has a small set of appropriate forms.

- **Comparison:** which is larger, and by how much? Answer with position on a common scale, using a sorted bar chart, a dot plot, or a slope chart for two points in time. Bars work because length encodes the value against a shared baseline.
- **Part-to-whole:** how does this break down? Answer with a stacked bar, which beats a pie once there are more than two or three segments because people compare lengths better than areas, or a treemap for many categories, with segments kept in order.
- **Distribution:** how is it spread? Answer with a histogram, a box plot, or a strip of dots. Skipping this shape is the most damaging omission in business decks, because an average alone hides the bimodality that matters.
- **Relationship:** do these two move together? Answer with a scatterplot, and add a trend line only when the relationship is the point and both scales are labelled honestly.
- **Change over time:** what is the direction and the shape? Answer with a line chart for continuous series, a column chart for discrete periods with few points, and a slope chart for exactly two points. Do not use a line chart for unordered categories, because the connecting line implies continuity that does not exist.

A sixth case is often overlooked: **rank against a target**, where a bullet chart, or a simple bar with a target line, beats both a table and a gauge.

The mapping is not mechanical. A question can have two valid forms, and the tie is broken by what the audience must do with the answer. If they must judge magnitude against a target, put the target on the chart. If they must notice a change, put the change in the title. If they must look up a specific value, use a table and stop pretending it is a chart.

One diagnostic catches most errors: write the question in one sentence, in the words the audience would use, then write down what the audience must do with the answer. Choose the form that makes that action easy. If the answer is "nothing, they only need to see that it exists", the correct form is a single number, not a chart.
principles: Write the audience's question in their words before choosing any chart form.
Choose the form that makes the audience's required action easy, not the form your data suggests.
Use bars for magnitude comparison, stacked bars for composition, and histograms for distribution, because each encodes on a channel the eye reads well.
Never connect discrete categories with a line; the line implies a continuity you do not have.
Include a distribution somewhere in every metrics review, because the average is where bad news hides.

pitfalls.failure: Using a pie chart for four or more segments, so the reader has to compare angles to find the largest slice.
pitfalls.fix: Convert to a sorted bar chart or a stacked bar, keeping the ordering the same as the message.

pitfalls.failure: Reporting only an average or a single KPI when the interesting variation is inside the distribution.
pitfalls.fix: Add a histogram or a percentile breakdown next to the mean, and say which segment the number hides.

pitfalls.failure: Reusing the same chart form for every slide so the deck looks consistent, at the cost of answering the question in front of it.
pitfalls.fix: Let the question choose the form. Consistency of message and title style matters; consistency of form does not.

concepts.title: The One-Message Chart: Titles That State the Finding, and the 'So What?' Annotation
concepts.summary: A chart with two messages has none. Write the claim as the title, then add a single annotation that answers 'so what?' so the audience does not have to supply the implication themselves.
concepts.detail:
Two rules do most of the work in a data-driven talk, and both are cheap to apply.

**One message per chart.** A chart that tries to show a trend, a segment mix, and a variance at once is making the audience do three readings simultaneously, and they will do none of them. The number of charts in a deck is not a measure of evidence; the number of claims per chart is a measure of confusion. If a chart genuinely supports two findings, split it into two charts, or keep one chart and make the second finding a sentence.

**The title that states the message.** The conventional chart title names the subject: "Net revenue retention by segment." The message title names the finding: "Enterprise NRR is 128 percent; self-serve is 94 percent, and it is one third of revenue." This is a small change with a large effect, because the audience reads titles first, in parallel, and a finding-title is a sentence the room can repeat in the hallway. It also forces the author to finish the thinking. If you cannot write a finding-title, you have not decided what the chart is for, and the audience will not decide for you.

**The 'So what?' annotation.** One short line on or next to the chart stating the implication, the action, or the caveat. It is the difference between showing data and making a point, and it should read like a speaker would say it: "This is the cohort we are losing, and it is the pricing change from March." Not "Note: Q3 data." Not a restatement of the title. The annotation is also the cheapest credibility available in a deck, because saying "the March cohort is only eleven accounts" in your own annotation is very different from the same fact emerging in Q&A.

The three pieces work as a unit: the message title tells the room what to take away, the chart gives the shape of the evidence, and the annotation says what it means and what to watch. Charts missing one of the three fail differently. A chart with a finding-title and no annotation leaves the implication to the room. A chart with an annotation and a subject title makes the audience work backwards. A chart with neither is wallpaper.
principles: One claim per chart; if two claims are real, split the chart.
Write the title as the finding the audience should repeat, not the name of the dataset.
Add one annotation that states the implication, the action, or the caveat, in plain words.
Put the caveat in your own annotation rather than waiting for someone else to find it.
A chart without a message title is a chart you have not finished designing.

pitfalls.failure: Titles that name the metric and force the room to supply the conclusion, such as 'Churn by cohort, FY26 Q1 to Q3'.
pitfalls.fix: Write the conclusion first, then check that the chart actually supports it. 'Churn rose in exactly one cohort, and it is our largest enterprise renewal cohort.'

pitfalls.failure: An annotation that restates the title in different words, adding length without adding information.
pitfalls.fix: Ask what the audience would ask next, and answer that. Often it is the action, often it is the caveat, never the restatement.

pitfalls.failure: Dropping the one-message rule under time pressure, so a single busy chart carries four findings in a rushed deck.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the headline chart and move the supporting detail to the appendix. One legible chart beats four crowded ones, and a rushed deck needs legible more than it needs complete.

concepts.title: The Honesty Trap: Truncated Axes, Wrong Denominators, Dual Axes, and the Credibility Bill
concepts.summary: The most common chart sins are not lies but distortions that let the reader draw a conclusion the data does not support. Getting caught doing one of them costs you the credibility of every other number in the deck.
concepts.detail:
A misleading chart is not always a lie. Most are distortions, and the dangerous ones are the kind a reasonable reader would never catch, which is why the speaker must catch them first. The inventory worth running before any chart ships:

- **Truncated axis.** A bar chart whose y-axis starts at 90 instead of 0 turns a 2 percent change into a dramatic climb. Bars encode value by length, so truncating a bar baseline breaks the encoding, not just the scale. A line chart may use a non-zero baseline, but the truncation must be unmistakable on the slide. The canonical public case is the 2005 hurricane-loss graphic in The New York Times, whose truncated axis drew sharp criticism, including from the statistician Danny Oppenheimer: a chart can be technically defensible and still mislead, because readers do not audit the encoding.
- **Wrong denominator.** "Churn is up 3 percent" against what base? A 3 percent increase on 40 customers is a different fact from 3 percent on 40,000. Changing the base from customers to revenue, or from new to total, changes the story without changing a point.
- **3D anything.** Perspective distorts area and length, so the picture contradicts the printed number: chartjunk that also lies.
- **Dual axes.** Two y-axes with independently chosen scales can be tuned to show any correlation you like, including one you know is spurious. Index both series to a common baseline, or use two panels.
- **Misleading scale in either direction.** Truncation and compression are the same error: a 300 percent increase in a segment of nine accounts needs its base printed beside it.
- **Category omission.** Starting a bar chart at the third-largest segment, with no sign two larger ones exist, is the same distortion in costume.

The credibility bill is the part executives underrate. It is not for the offending chart. It is for every other number you have shown that room, and every number you will show them next. A room that catches one truncated axis does not merely discount that chart; it re-audits everything, visibly, so the rest of the deck is now read adversarially by people who were reading it charitably a moment ago.

The defensive posture does not work; there is no good way to say 'that is just how we plot it'. The only cheap defence is to audit your own charts first, and to design the honest version to be the persuasive one, which is usually possible: a bar chart starting at zero is not less persuasive, only less dramatic, and the claim that survives it is the one you were entitled to make anyway.
principles: Bars must start at zero; lines may truncate only if the truncation is unmistakable on the slide.
Print the base with every percentage change, every rate, and every 'up' or 'down' claim.
Never use 3D on a chart whose values may be quoted, and never use dual axes to manufacture a relationship.
Audit each chart by asking what a hostile reader could claim you hid, then fix it before you present.
Design the honest version to be the persuasive version, so integrity costs you nothing.

pitfalls.failure: Truncating a bar axis because the untruncated version does not make the point, and hoping nobody checks.
pitfalls.fix: Start at zero and make the claim in the title instead. If the honest chart does not support the claim, the claim is wrong.

pitfalls.failure: Quoting a change without its base, such as 'net new ARR grew 40 percent' when the base is three deals.
pitfalls.fix: Put the base in the sentence: 'Net new ARR grew 40 percent, on three deals last quarter against eleven the quarter before.'

pitfalls.failure: Defending a questionable chart when it is challenged, which converts a formatting choice into a character issue.
pitfalls.fix: Concede the encoding, point to the underlying data, and offer the untruncated version. 'Here is the same data with a zero baseline, and the conclusion holds.'

concepts.title: The Exec Number Set: The Three to Five Numbers a Board Actually Needs
concepts.summary: Boards do not need more data, they need a small set of numbers they can hold. Choosing three to five, giving each one a job, and cutting the rest is a discipline that takes longer than it sounds.
concepts.detail:
Ask a board what they want to see and you will get everything. A board agenda is a request for a complete operating picture, and completeness is what kills the meeting. The Exec Number Set is the discipline of choosing three to five numbers, giving each one a specific job in the story, and cutting the rest into an appendix.

Each surviving number must do exactly one of four jobs, and no number may do two:

1. **The scale number.** How big is the business. Revenue, ARR, users, volume, bookings. One number, with a comparison the room can make sense of, and ideally a trend.
2. **The health number.** Is the business getting better or worse in the way that matters. Retention, churn, gross margin, burn multiple, cycle time. One number.
3. **The engine number.** The one thing that is working and is worth copying. New logos, expansion, activation, a segment that is compounding.
4. **The bet number.** What the company is deliberately spending to get somewhere. Headcount in a new function, R&D, a new market, a price change. One number, and it is usually the one that is hardest to defend.

Four numbers, four jobs, and the set is legible in under ten seconds. Most executive decks run eight to fifteen numbers, and the cost is not confusion exactly; it is dilution. When every number is highlighted, none is. The room cannot tell which one you wanted them to act on, so they discuss the most recent one, which is usually the most volatile one.

The cut is the hard part, and the test for whether you cut enough is this: if you removed a number from the set, would anyone in the room notice its absence? If not, it was not in the set, it was in the way. Cutting is also a claim, so expect pushback from the team whose number you removed. Handle it by moving it to the appendix and saying so in the room: 'The full operating dashboard is in the appendix; the four numbers on the slide are the ones I need a decision on today.'

Two further rules. Give each number a direction and a horizon, a prior period and a target, so improvement is legible. And keep the set stable across meetings: if the numbers change every quarter, the board cannot track anything, and the deck becomes a quarterly novelty rather than a scoreboard.

There is a legitimate exception: in a diligence or crisis conversation, a broader set may be necessary. The discipline still applies, but the scope changes. What does not change is that the room must be able to say, at the end, what you wanted them to decide.
principles: Choose three to five numbers and give each one exactly one job: scale, health, engine, or bet.
Give every number a direction and a horizon so the room knows what improving looks like.
Move everything else to the appendix and say so in the room; a visible cut is a claim about what matters.
Keep the set stable across meetings so the board can track it quarter over quarter.
One number may not do two jobs; if a number is both your health metric and your growth story, pick one.

pitfalls.failure: Highlighting every number in the deck, so the room cannot tell which one you wanted them to act on.
pitfalls.fix: Use one accent colour and one style for the numbers that carry the message; everything else goes to neutral grey and the appendix.

pitfalls.failure: Letting a metric owner's number into the set because it is interesting rather than decision-relevant.
pitfalls.fix: Apply the removal test: if nobody would notice its absence, it goes to the appendix, regardless of who owns it.

pitfalls.failure: Changing the set every quarter, so no one can tell whether the business is actually improving.
pitfalls.fix: Fix the set for the fiscal year and treat changes as an explicit, explained decision rather than a default.
